questions.stem:
A non-pipelined instruction execution unit that operates at 1.6 GHz clock takes an average of 5 clock cycles to complete the execution of an instruction. To improve the performance, the system was pipelined with a goal of achieving an average throughput of one instruction per clock cycle. However, it could operate only at 1.2 GHz due to pipeline overheads. While executing a program in the pipelined design, 30% of instructions encountered a stall of 2 cycles due to pipeline hazards. The speed-up obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined one for this program is ___________. (rounded off to two decimal places)

Note: $1\mathrm{G}=10^9$

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A clock cycle is one tick of the processor clock; a GHz figure is ticks per nanosecond. CPI (cycles per instruction) is the average number of ticks one instruction needs. A stall is a tick in which the pipeline completes nothing because an instruction must wait. Execution time per instruction is CPI times the clock period, and speed-up of design B over design A is the time per instruction of A divided by that of B. This one rule decides the question: compare time per instruction, never cycle counts alone, because the two designs run at different clock rates.

steps.title: Time per instruction, non-pipelined
steps.body: CPI is 5 and the clock is 1.6 GHz, so the period is $1/1.6=0.625$ ns. Each instruction takes $5\times0.625$ ns.

steps.title: Time per instruction, pipelined
steps.body: Ideal CPI is 1. Thirty percent of instructions lose 2 cycles each, so on average $0.3\times2=0.6$ extra cycles are added. The effective CPI is 1.6. The clock is only 1.2 GHz, so the period is $1/1.2$ ns.

steps.title: Divide
steps.body: Speed-up is $3.125/1.3333=2.34375$, which rounds to 2.34. The official range 2.30 to 2.40 contains it.

shortcut.body: Write time per instruction as CPI over frequency for both designs and divide: $(5/1.6)\,/\,(1.6/1.2)$. Ten seconds with a calculator. Safe whenever both clock rates are given.

traps.text: Scaling the cycle ratio by the frequency ratio the wrong way, $(5/1.6)\times(1.6/1.2)=4.17$. The faster non-pipelined clock must make its time per instruction smaller, so the 1.2 GHz period goes in the denominator of the pipelined time, not the numerator of the ratio.
Treating the speed-up as 5 / 1.6 = 3.125 ignores the slower clock and gives a value above the range.
Applying the 2-cycle stall to all instructions gives CPI 3 and a speed-up of 1.25; only 30% stall.

recognize.clues: Two designs with different clock rates, an average cycle count for one, and a fraction of instructions that stall for a fixed number of cycles in the other.
recognize.contrast: Not the cycle-time formula with latch delay: no stage delays are given, so the clock is a stated frequency and the work is in the CPI with stalls.

check.body: Work in cycles of the faster clock instead. In 1.2 GHz ticks the non-pipelined unit needs 5 x 1.2/1.6 = 3.75 ticks per instruction, and the pipelined unit needs 1.6. The ratio 3.75/1.6 is the same 2.34 from a different route.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2026 CS-2 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: The two designs run at different clock rates. What single quantity lets you say one finishes an instruction sooner than the other?
Cycles per instruction (CPI) counts clock ticks per instruction, and the clock period turns ticks into nanoseconds.
Time per instruction is CPI divided by the clock frequency, and speed-up compares the old time to the new time.
For the pipelined design start from the ideal CPI of 1 and add stall cycles weighted by the fraction of instructions that suffer them.
The non-pipelined unit needs 5 ticks of a 1.6 GHz clock for each instruction; convert that into nanoseconds before touching the pipelined side.

variation.stem: A non-pipelined unit runs at 2 GHz and takes an average of 4 cycles per instruction. A pipelined redesign has an ideal CPI of 1 but can only run at 1.5 GHz. In the program, 25% of instructions stall for 3 cycles. What is the speed-up of the pipelined design over the non-pipelined one, rounded to two decimal places?
variation.explanation: Non-pipelined time per instruction is 4/2 = 2 ns. Pipelined CPI is 1 + 0.25 x 3 = 1.75, so its time is 1.75/1.5 = 1.1667 ns. The speed-up is 2/1.1667 = 1.71. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: Which one of the following dependencies among the register operands of different instructions can cause a data hazard in a pipelined processor?
options: Read-after-read
Read-after-write
Write-after-read
Write-after-write

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A data hazard arises when two instructions touch the same register and overlapping them in the pipeline could make one of them see a wrong value. Take instruction A before instruction B in program order. Read-after-write (RAW): B reads what A writes, so B must wait for A. Write-after-read (WAR): B writes what A reads. Write-after-write (WAW): both write the same register. Read-after-read (RAR): both only read. The rule: a hazard needs at least one write, and in a simple in-order 5-stage pipeline the one that really bites is RAW because a later reader can reach its read stage before the earlier writer has written back.

steps.title: Test each pair
steps.body: RAR: neither instruction changes the register, so the value cannot differ; no hazard. RAW: instruction B reads in ID (cycle 3 when B follows A directly), but A writes only in WB (cycle 5), two cycles later, so B can read a stale value; this is a true data hazard. WAR and WAW are name dependences. They can bite only if instructions are reordered or finish out of order, which an in-order pipeline with one write stage does not do.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: Among the four, read-after-write is the dependency that causes a data hazard in the pipelined processor: option B.

shortcut.body: RAW is the true dependence: the second instruction needs a value the first has not yet produced. If an option says "read-after-write", pick it; read-after-read is never a hazard.

traps.text: Read-after-read involves no write, so there is no value to get wrong. Candidates pick it because both instructions use the same register.
Write-after-read is a hazard only when a later write can overtake an earlier read, which cannot happen in an in-order pipeline with fixed read and write stages.
Write-after-write needs two writes to land in the wrong order; in the classic 5-stage pipeline all writes happen in WB in program order, so it only matters with out-of-order completion.

recognize.clues: The wording lists four register dependency names and asks which one causes a data hazard in a pipelined processor.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse true dependences with name dependences: a later read of a value an earlier instruction writes needs the new value, while write-first-order pairs only matter when completion is out of order.

check.body: Test with a concrete pair: ADD R1,R2,R3 then SUB R4,R1,R5. SUB reads R1 in cycle 3 but ADD writes R1 in cycle 5, so SUB would read the old value. Replace the second instruction by one that merely reads R2 again and nothing can go wrong.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2026 CS-1 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: Look at what each option does to the register: which of the four dependencies could hand a later instruction a stale value?
A data hazard is two instructions sharing a register in a way that overlapping them could change what one of them sees.
A value can only go wrong if someone changes it, so a pair with no write at all can never hurt; among the pairs with a write, ask which one a fixed-stage in-order pipeline can actually reorder.
Mark which stage reads a register and which stage writes one, then ask for each option whether the later instruction can reach its access before the earlier one has finished its own.

variation.stem: Consider the in-order 5-stage pipeline with the sequence I1: LD R2, 0(R1); I2: ADD R4, R2, R3; I3: SUB R5, R3, R6. Which dependency below can make an instruction read a stale value if no stall or forwarding is used?
options: I2 and I3, read-after-read on R3
I1 and I3, write-after-read on R6
I1 and I2, read-after-write on R2
I1 and I3, write-after-write on R5
variation.explanation: I1 writes R2 in WB and I2 reads R2 in ID two cycles earlier, so this read-after-write pair is a true hazard. I2 and I3 only read R3, so nothing changes. I1 and I3 share no register at all, so options B and D name dependences that do not exist. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
The EX stage of a pipelined processor performs the memory read operations for LOAD instructions, and the operations for the arithmetic and logic instructions. Let $t_{EX}$ denote the time taken by the EX stage to perform the operation for an instruction. For each instruction type, the values of $t_{EX}$ and M (the number of instructions of that type in a sequence of 100 instructions for a program P), are given in the table below.

The duration of the pipeline clock cycle is 1 nanosecond. Assume that the latch time for the interstage buffers in the pipeline is negligible.

When program P is executed, the number of clock cycles for which the pipeline is stalled due to structural hazards in the EX stage is ______. (answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: Bars of EX time for each instruction type against 1 ns cycle lines; stalls per type are cycles minus one, times M, totalling 95.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A pipeline clock cycle is the fixed time each stage gets. If a stage needs longer than one cycle for some instruction, that instruction occupies the stage for several cycles, and the single unit cannot accept the next instruction meanwhile. That conflict over one shared resource is a structural hazard, and every extra cycle the pipeline waits is one stall cycle. The rule: an operation of length $t$ ns on a 1 ns clock holds the stage for $\lceil t\rceil$ cycles, so it causes $\lceil t\rceil-1$ stall cycles.

steps.title: Cycles held per type
steps.body: Round each $t_{EX}$ up to a whole number of 1 ns cycles: LOAD 1.8 gives 2, IMUL 1.5 gives 2, IDIV 2.5 gives 3, FADD 1.7 gives 2, FSUB 1.7 gives 2, FMUL 2.8 gives 3, FDIV 3.2 gives 4. The other 35 instructions are under 1 ns and fit in one cycle, so they add no stall.

steps.title: Multiply by how many of each
steps.body: Stalls per instruction times the count M: LOAD $1\times15$, IMUL $1\times10$, IDIV $2\times5$, FADD $1\times10$, FSUB $1\times5$, FMUL $2\times15$, FDIV $3\times5$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The pipeline is stalled for 95 cycles because of structural hazards in the EX stage. The drawing shows each type against the 1 ns cycle boundaries.

shortcut.body: Compute ceil(t) minus 1 for each type, multiply by M and add. Mental check by grouping: 1-stall types (LOAD, IMUL, FADD, FSUB) have 15+10+10+5=40 instructions, 2-stall types 20, 3-stall types 5, so $40+40+15$. Unsafe if the question asked for total cycles instead of stalls.

traps.text: Using ceil(t) instead of ceil(t) minus 1 counts the one cycle every instruction already needs. That gives 95 + 65 = 160, since 65 instructions need more than one cycle.
Rounding down (floor) loses the spill-over: 1.8 ns would be 1 cycle and no stall, which gives a number far below 95.
Counting the 35 fast instructions as stalls. They finish within one cycle and never block the EX unit.

recognize.clues: One EX stage serves every instruction, the EX times differ by type and exceed the 1 ns clock, and the question asks for stall cycles over a mix of 100 instructions.
recognize.contrast: Not a data-hazard stall count: nothing here depends on register values. The stalls come from the unit being busy, so they are counted from the operation time.

check.body: Bound the answer without rounding. If each operation were charged its exact extra time $t-1$ ns, the stalls would be $15(0.8)+10(0.5)+5(1.5)+10(0.7)+5(0.7)+15(1.8)+5(2.2)=73$ cycles. Rounding up to whole cycles adds less than one cycle for each of the 65 slow instructions, so the true count lies between 73 and 138. The result 95 sits inside that range.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2026 CS-1 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: What happens to the pipeline when one instruction needs the EX unit for longer than one clock cycle?
A single EX unit that is busy for several cycles cannot accept the next instruction meanwhile, which is a structural hazard.
An operation that takes $t$ ns on a clock of period $T$ holds the stage for the next whole number of cycles at or above $t/T$, and only the cycles beyond the first are stalls.
Make a list per instruction type of cycles held minus one, multiply each by its count M, and add. Types under one cycle contribute nothing.
Take the LOAD row: 1.8 ns on a 1 ns clock occupies EX for two cycles, so each LOAD costs one stall; scale that by 15 instructions.

variation.stem: In a pipeline the EX stage handles every operation, and the clock cycle is 2 ns. For a sequence of 100 instructions the EX times are: LOAD 3.5 ns (20 instructions), IMUL 4.2 ns (10), FADD 2.0 ns (10), FDIV 6.5 ns (5), and all other instructions less than 2 ns (55). How many cycles is the pipeline stalled because of structural hazards in the EX stage?
variation.explanation: Cycles held are the ceiling of t/2: LOAD 2, IMUL 3, FADD 1 (exactly one cycle, no stall), FDIV 4. Stalls per instruction are 1, 2, 0 and 3, so the total is 1x20 + 2x10 + 0x10 + 3x5 = 55. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 180, 250, 150, 170, and 250, respectively, in nanoseconds. The delay of an inter-stage latch is 10 nanoseconds. Assume that there are no pipeline stalls due to branches and other hazards. The time taken to process 1000 instructions in microseconds is __________ . (rounded off to two decimal places)

solutionDiagram.alt: Space-time chart of the 5-stage pipeline: each instruction starts one cycle after the previous; the cycle is 260 ns and 1000 instructions take 1004 cycles.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A pipeline splits an instruction into stages; all stages share one clock, so the clock period (cycle time) must fit the slowest stage. A latch is a register between stages that holds the partial result; it adds its own delay to every cycle. With no stalls, the first instruction takes $k$ cycles to travel through $k$ stages, and after that one instruction finishes every cycle. The rule is the pair of formulas below.

steps.title: Cycle time
steps.body: The slowest stage is 250 ns, and the latch adds 10 ns.

steps.title: Number of cycles
steps.body: There are $k=5$ stages and $n=1000$ instructions, so $5+999=1004$ cycles.

steps.title: Total time and unit
steps.body: $1004\times260=261040$ ns. The question wants microseconds, and 1000 ns is 1 microsecond, so the answer is 261.04.

shortcut.body: (k + n - 1) times (slowest + latch) = 1004 x 260 = 261040 ns; divide by 1000 for microseconds. Unsafe only if stalls or a non-pipelined baseline are mentioned.

traps.text: Using 1000 x 5 x 260 = 1,300,000 ns counts every instruction as taking the full pipeline depth, which defeats overlapping.
Forgetting the latch gives (1004 x 250) / 1000 = 251.00.
Using n cycles, 1000 x 260 ns = 260.00, drops the 4 cycles of filling the pipeline.
Leaving the answer in ns (261040) when the question asks for microseconds.

recognize.clues: Stage delays differ, an inter-stage latch delay is given, there are no stalls, and the total time for a long run of instructions is asked.
recognize.contrast: Not the speed-up question: no non-pipelined baseline is asked for, only the pipelined total time, so the k + n - 1 cycle count is used directly.

check.body: Check against the limit. For a very long run the time per instruction tends to one cycle, 260 ns, so 1000 instructions should cost a little more than 260 microseconds. A result just above that, not 1300 or 251, is consistent.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: Which stage limits how fast the clock can tick, and does anything besides the stages add to each tick?
All stages share one clock, so the period has to fit the slowest stage plus the latch between stages.
With no stalls, the first instruction needs one cycle per stage and after that one instruction completes every cycle.
Find the cycle time, count the cycles for 1000 instructions on a pipeline of this depth, multiply, then convert nanoseconds to microseconds.
The slowest stage is 250 ns and the latch adds 10 ns, which fixes the period of every cycle; now count how many such cycles are needed.

variation.stem: A 6-stage pipeline has stage delays of 90, 140, 110, 140, 120 and 100 ns, and each inter-stage latch adds 10 ns. There are no stalls. How many microseconds does it take to process 500 instructions? Give the answer to two decimal places.
variation.explanation: The cycle is the slowest stage plus the latch, 140 + 10 = 150 ns. The number of cycles is 6 + 500 - 1 = 505. The time is 505 x 150 = 75750 ns, which is 75.75 microseconds. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
An instruction format has the following structure:

Instruction Number: Opcode destination reg, source reg-1, source reg-2

Consider the following sequence of instructions to be executed in a pipelined processor:

I1: DIV R3, R1, R2
I2: SUB R5, R3, R4
I3: ADD R3, R5, R6
I4: MUL R7, R3, R8

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: There is a RAW dependency on R3 between I1 and I2
There is a WAR dependency on R3 between I1 and I3
There is a RAW dependency on R3 between I2 and I3
There is a WAW dependency on R3 between I3 and I4

solutionDiagram.alt: Dependency graph of I1 to I4: RAW on R3 from I1 to I2, RAW on R5 from I2 to I3, WAW on R3 from I1 to I3, WAR on R3 from I2 to I3, RAW on R3 from I3 to I4.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: In an instruction the destination register is written and the two source registers are read. For two instructions X (earlier) and Y (later) that use the same register: RAW (read-after-write) means Y reads what X writes; WAR (write-after-read) means Y writes what X reads; WAW (write-after-write) means both write it. The register named in each statement and the instruction pair decide whether it is true. The destination is the first register after the opcode.

steps.title: Write down what each instruction reads and writes
steps.body: I1 writes R3, reads R1 and R2. I2 writes R5, reads R3 and R4. I3 writes R3, reads R5 and R6. I4 writes R7, reads R3 and R8.
steps.tex: \begin{array}{c|cc} & \text{writes} & \text{reads}\\\hline I_1 & R3 & R1,R2\\ I_2 & R5 & R3,R4\\ I_3 & R3 & R5,R6\\ I_4 & R7 & R3,R8\end{array}

steps.title: Check the four statements
steps.body: (A) I1 writes R3 and I2 reads R3: RAW on R3, true. (B) I1 and I3 both write R3, so it is WAW, not WAR; false. (C) I2 writes R5, not R3; the I2-I3 RAW is on R5, and on R3 the I2-I3 pair is WAR; false. (D) I3 writes R3 and I4 reads R3, so it is RAW, not WAW; false.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only statement A is true.

shortcut.body: List for each instruction what it writes (first register) and reads (the other two). A pair is RAW if the earlier writes and the later reads the register, WAW if both write, WAR if the earlier reads and the later writes. Takes one minute for four instructions.

traps.text: Calling the I1 and I3 pair WAR: both write R3, which is WAW. WAR would need I1 to read R3.
The RAW between I2 and I3 exists, but on R5 (I2 writes R5, I3 reads it), not on R3. The statement names the wrong register.
I3 writes R3 and I4 reads it, which is RAW. Both instructions would have to write R3 for WAW.

recognize.clues: A four-instruction sequence with destination and source registers, and statements that each name a dependency type, a register and a pair of instructions.
recognize.contrast: RAW, WAR and WAW look alike; tell them apart by which of the two instructions writes the register and which reads it.

check.body: Check a false statement by counting writers. Statement D names a WAW on R3 for I3 and I4, but I4 writes R7 only, so there is just one writer in that pair and a WAW cannot exist.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2024 CS2 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: For each statement, which instruction writes the named register and which only reads it?
The first register after the opcode is the destination, written; the other two are sources, read.
For an earlier and a later instruction, the order of write and read decides the name: write then read is RAW, read then write is WAR, write then write is WAW.
Make a small table of what each of the four instructions writes and reads, then test every statement against the exact pair and register it names.

variation.stem: Consider the sequence in a pipelined processor, where the first register is the destination: I1: ADD R1, R2, R3; I2: MUL R4, R1, R5; I3: SUB R1, R4, R6; I4: DIV R7, R1, R2. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: There is a WAR dependency on R1 between I1 and I3
There is a RAW dependency on R1 between I1 and I2
There is a WAR dependency on R1 between I2 and I3
There is a WAW dependency on R1 between I3 and I4
variation.explanation: I1 writes R1 and I2 reads it, so B is a RAW. I2 reads R1 and I3 writes it, so C is a WAR. I1 and I3 both write R1, so that pair is WAW, not WAR. I4 reads R1 instead of writing it, so I3 and I4 form a RAW, not a WAW. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: A non-pipelined instruction execution unit operating at 2 GHz takes an average of 6 cycles to execute an instruction of a program P. The unit is then redesigned to operate on a 5-stage pipeline at 2 GHz. Assume that the ideal throughput of the pipelined unit is 1 instruction per cycle. In the execution of program P, 20% instructions incur an average of 2 cycles stall due to data hazards and 20% instructions incur an average of 3 cycles stall due to control hazards. The speedup (rounded off to one decimal place) obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined design is _________

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: CPI is the average number of clock cycles per instruction. A data hazard stall is a wait for an operand; a control hazard stall is a wait after a branch for the next correct instruction. Stalls add to the ideal CPI of 1, weighted by the fraction of instructions that suffer them. With equal clock rates, speed-up is the ratio of CPIs.

steps.title: Pipelined CPI
steps.body: Data hazards add $0.2\times2=0.4$ cycles, control hazards add $0.2\times3=0.6$ cycles per instruction.

steps.title: Speed-up
steps.body: Both designs run at 2 GHz, so the clock cancels. Non-pipelined CPI is 6.

shortcut.body: Same clock, so speed-up = 6 / (1 + 0.2x2 + 0.2x3) = 6 / 2 = 3.0 in one line. If the clocks differed, divide each CPI by its frequency first.

traps.text: Adding the two stalls as 2 + 3 = 5 for every instruction gives CPI 6 and speed-up 1.0; only 20% of instructions stall for each cause.
Forgetting the ideal CPI of 1 gives 6 / 1.0 = 6.0.
Using 5 (the pipeline depth) as the non-pipelined CPI gives 2.5; the question states 6 cycles.

recognize.clues: A non-pipelined average cycle count, an ideal pipelined throughput of one per cycle, and fractions of instructions that incur stalls from two different hazard causes.
recognize.contrast: Not the Amdahl style speed-up: the gain comes from overlapping, with its loss counted in stall cycles, not from a parallel fraction of the program.

check.body: Per 100 instructions: 100 ideal cycles, 20 x 2 = 40 data stalls and 20 x 3 = 60 control stalls give 200 cycles pipelined, against 600 cycles non-pipelined. The ratio of 600 to 200 is the same.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2024 CS2 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: Both designs run at 2 GHz. What does that let you do with the clock when comparing them?
Speed-up of one design over another is the ratio of their average times per instruction, which here reduces to a ratio of CPIs.
Pipelined CPI is the ideal CPI plus, for every hazard source, the fraction of instructions affected times the stall cycles each suffers.
Handle the data hazards and control hazards as two separate terms, add both to the ideal CPI, then divide the non-pipelined CPI by the result.
The data hazards add 20% of 2 cycles per instruction on average; work out the control hazard term the same way before adding.

variation.stem: A non-pipelined unit running at 3 GHz takes an average of 7 cycles per instruction. It is redesigned as a pipeline at 3 GHz with an ideal throughput of one instruction per cycle. In the program, 15% of instructions stall for 2 cycles because of data hazards and 20% stall for 4 cycles because of control hazards. What is the speed-up, rounded to two decimal places?
variation.explanation: The clock is equal, so only CPI matters. Pipelined CPI is 1 + 0.15 x 2 + 0.20 x 4 = 2.1. The speed-up is 7/2.1 = 3.33. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?
options: In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction
In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the input of the EX stage of the next instruction
Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls
Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the pipeline stages

solutionDiagram.alt: Chart of a load and a dependent add: the loaded value is forwarded from the end of MEM in cycle 4 to the start of EX in cycle 5, leaving one stall cycle.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: Forwarding (bypassing) is extra wiring that sends a result straight from a pipeline register at the end of one stage to the input of an earlier stage of a following instruction, so it does not wait for the write to the register file in WB. It exists to shorten the stall caused by a read-after-write dependency. The rule for judging each statement: a result can be forwarded only from the cycle in which it exists, and the wires and multiplexers that carry it are real hardware.

steps.title: Statements A and B
steps.body: A describes exactly what forwarding is: the result of an earlier instruction, at a source stage, goes to a destination stage of a later one. True. B: a loaded value appears at the end of MEM, and the next instruction (after one stall) takes it at the input of its EX stage. True.

steps.title: Statements C and D
steps.body: C: a load followed by a dependent instruction still stalls one cycle even with forwarding, because the data is not available until the end of MEM (see the chart). True. D: forwarding needs multiplexers at the ALU inputs, comparators and bypass paths from the pipeline registers; so claiming no extra hardware is false.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: A, B and C are correct.

shortcut.body: Eliminate by the hardware fact: forwarding always costs multiplexers and bypass wires, so D is out. A is the definition, B and C are standard facts about load-use. Safe because the other three are textbook statements.

traps.text: Believing forwarding is free. The bypass paths, multiplexers and hazard-detection comparators are extra hardware, which is the price of the speed-up.
Thinking forwarding removes every stall. The load-use hazard still costs one cycle, and a branch outcome is not helped by data forwarding.

recognize.clues: Statements about forwarding in a 5-stage pipeline: where the data comes from, where it goes, whether stalls vanish and whether hardware is needed.
recognize.contrast: Forwarding is not stall insertion: forwarding shortens the wait for a value, while a stall delays the instruction. A load-use pair still needs both.

check.body: Check the load-use claim by timing. The load runs IF in cycle 1, ID 2, EX 3, MEM 4, so its data exists only at the end of cycle 4. The next instruction runs IF 2, ID 3 and would start EX in cycle 4, one cycle too early. It must wait and start EX in cycle 5, so one stall remains even with forwarding.

GATE 2024 CS1 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: What does forwarding actually hand over, from where, and to where? Judge each statement against that picture.
Forwarding sends a result from a pipeline register to an earlier stage of a following instruction instead of waiting for the register file write.
Ask what must physically exist for a result to reach an earlier stage, and in which cycle the value first exists.
Draw two dependent instructions in a 5-stage chart and mark the cycle in which the first result first exists and the cycle in which the second would first want it.

variation.stem: A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) uses full forwarding. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
options: An ALU result can be forwarded from the end of EX to the input of EX of the next instruction
A load followed immediately by an instruction using its value needs no stall with full forwarding
Forwarding removes the need for the register file write in WB
Forwarding by itself does not shorten the stall after a taken branch
variation.explanation: An ALU result exists at the end of EX, so the next instruction can take it at its EX input with no stall. A loaded value appears only at the end of MEM, so a load-use pair still stalls one cycle. The register file must still be written. Forwarding moves data only, not the branch outcome. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
The baseline execution time of a program on a 2 GHz single core machine is 100 nanoseconds (ns). The code corresponding to 90% of the execution time can be fully parallelized. The overhead for using an additional core is 10 ns when running on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share of the parallelized code for an equal amount of time.

The number of cores that minimize the execution time of the program is ________

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: Speed-up by parallelism is limited by the part that cannot be split (Amdahl's law). Here 90 ns of the 100 ns is parallelizable and 10 ns is serial. With $n$ cores the parallel part takes $90/n$ ns, but each core beyond the first costs 10 ns of overhead, so adding cores helps at first and then hurts. The rule is to write total time as a function of $n$ and take the smallest value.

steps.title: Evaluate for small n
steps.body: $T(1)=100$, $T(2)=10+45+10=65$, $T(3)=10+30+20=60$, $T(4)=10+22.5+30=62.5$, $T(5)=10+18+40=68$. After $n=4$ the overhead term grows faster than the saving, so the time keeps rising.

steps.title: Check by calculus and answer
steps.body: Setting the slope of $90/n+10n$ to zero gives $n^2=9$, so $n=3$, a whole number, which matches the table. The minimum is 60 ns at 3 cores.

shortcut.body: The sum 90/n + 10n is smallest when the two terms are equal in size: 90/n = 10, so n squared = 9 and n = 3. Safe when the optimum is an integer; otherwise compare the two nearest integers.

traps.text: Charging the overhead for n cores instead of n - 1 gives T = 10 + 90/n + 10n, still minimal at n = 3 but with the wrong time of 70 ns instead of 60 ns. The core count survives; the time does not.
Dropping the overhead and answering with the largest core count, since 90/n always falls.
Dropping the serial 10 ns gives T = 90/n + 10(n - 1): 90, 55, 50, 52.5 for n = 1 to 4. The core count is still 3 but the time is 50 ns, not 60 ns.

recognize.clues: A fixed baseline time, a fraction that can be split across cores, and a per-core overhead, with the number of cores to be chosen to minimise time.
recognize.contrast: This is Amdahl's law with an extra cost per core, so unlike the plain law the time does not fall forever; it has a minimum at a finite core count.

check.body: Substitute the neighbours. At n = 2 the time is 65 ns, at n = 3 it is 60 ns and at n = 4 it is 62.5 ns. The middle value is the smallest of the three, so the choice holds on both sides.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2024 CS1 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: Adding cores shrinks one part of the time and grows another. What are the two competing parts?
Only the parallelizable part divides across cores, and every core after the first adds a fixed overhead.
To minimise a sum of a falling term and a rising term, look for the place where adding one more core stops paying off.
Write total time as a function of the core count n with the serial time, the parallel time divided by n and the overhead term, then compare neighbouring integers.
The serial part is the 10 ns left over after the 90 ns that can be parallelized; keep it as a constant term.

variation.stem: A program takes 200 ns on a single core. 80% of its execution time can be fully parallelized and the rest is serial. Each additional core beyond the first adds an overhead of 10 ns. Assuming all cores share the parallel work equally, how many cores minimize the execution time?
variation.explanation: Total time is T(n) = 40 + 160/n + 10(n - 1). T(3) = 113.3, T(4) = 110 and T(5) = 112, so the minimum is at 4 cores. The same value comes from setting 160/n^2 = 10, giving n = 4. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
Consider a 3-stage pipelined processor having a delay of 10 ns (nanoseconds), 20 ns, and 14 ns, for the first, second, and the third stages, respectively. Assume that there is no other delay and the processor does not suffer from any pipeline hazards. Also assume that one instruction is fetched every cycle.

The total execution time for executing 100 instructions on this processor is ______ ns.

solutionDiagram.alt: Space-time chart of three stages with a 20 ns cycle: each instruction starts one cycle later; 100 instructions take 3 plus 99 equals 102 cycles.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A pipeline stage is one step of instruction processing, and a pipeline overlaps the stages of different instructions. All stages are driven by one clock, so the clock period must be as long as the slowest stage. Hazards are situations that force waiting; none occur here. With $k$ stages and $n$ instructions, the first needs $k$ cycles and each later one finishes one cycle after the previous.

steps.title: Cycle time
steps.body: The slowest stage is the second, 20 ns, and there is no latch delay, so the cycle is 20 ns.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $k=3$ and $n=100$, so there are $3+99=102$ cycles, and $102\times20=2040$ ns.

shortcut.body: (3 + 99) x max stage delay = 102 x 20 = 2040. Unsafe only when a latch delay or stalls are mentioned.

traps.text: Using 100 x (10 + 20 + 14) = 4400 ns treats the processor as non-pipelined.
Using n cycles, 100 x 20 = 2000 ns, forgets the k - 1 cycles to fill the pipeline.
Taking the average stage delay (14.67 ns) as the cycle. The clock must fit the slowest stage.

recognize.clues: Stage delays given in ns with no latch delay, a stated absence of hazards, and a count of instructions to run in total.
recognize.contrast: A non-pipelined machine would add the three delays per instruction; the words "pipelined" and "no hazards" mean the time is beats times the slowest stage instead.

check.body: Second route: the first instruction leaves after 3 x 20 = 60 ns, and each of the other 99 leaves one 20 ns beat later, which adds 99 x 20 = 1980 ns to that 60 ns.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2023 CS answer key, IIT Kanpur (organising institute, PDF author IITK_GATE), IIT Guwahati archive copy

hints.text: What decides how often a new instruction can enter this pipeline, and how many of those beats pass before the last instruction is done?
All stages run off one clock, so the beat has to suit every stage, including the slowest one.
Once the pipe is full, one instruction finishes per beat; before that, the first instruction needs one beat for each stage.
Count the beats as the stages for the first instruction plus one more beat for each remaining instruction, then multiply by the beat length.

variation.stem: A 3-stage pipelined processor has stage delays of 12 ns, 18 ns and 15 ns. There is no other delay and no pipeline hazard, and one instruction is fetched every cycle. How many ns does it take to execute 50 instructions?
variation.explanation: The clock must fit the slowest stage, 18 ns. The pipeline needs 3 + 49 = 52 cycles, and 52 x 18 = 936 ns. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: A processor X1 operating at 2 GHz has a standard 5-stage RISC instruction pipeline having a base CPI (cycles per instruction) of one without any pipeline hazards. For a given program P that has 30% branch instructions, control hazards incur 2 cycles stall for every branch. A new version of the processor X2 operating at same clock frequency has an additional branch predictor unit (BPU) that completely eliminates stalls for correctly predicted branches. There is neither any savings nor any additional stalls for wrong predictions. There are no structural hazards and data hazards for X1 and X2. If the BPU has a prediction accuracy of 80%, the speed up (rounded off to two decimal places) obtained by X2 over X1 in executing P is____________.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A branch is an instruction that may change the next instruction to run. A control hazard is the wait while the pipeline does not yet know which instruction to fetch next. A branch predictor guesses the outcome early; a correct guess means no wait, a wrong guess pays the full penalty. The effective CPI is the base CPI plus the average stall per instruction, where average stall = branch fraction x fraction of branches that stall x penalty. Same clock, so speed-up is the CPI ratio.

steps.title: X1 without prediction
steps.body: Every branch stalls 2 cycles.

steps.title: X2 with 80% accurate prediction
steps.body: Only the 20% of branches predicted wrongly stall, and they stall the same 2 cycles.

steps.title: Speed-up
steps.body: $1.6/1.12=1.4286$, which rounds to 1.43. The official range is 1.42 to 1.45.

shortcut.body: Stall CPI: X1 adds 0.6, X2 adds 0.12. Speed-up = 1.6 / 1.12 = 1.43. Same clock, so no frequency factor.

traps.text: Using 0.8 as the stall probability (the accuracy instead of the error) gives CPI 1.48 and speed-up 1.08.
Using 1.6 / 1.0 = 1.6 assumes prediction removes every stall, but 20% of branches still pay the penalty.
Applying the 2-cycle penalty to all instructions rather than only the 30% that are branches.

recognize.clues: A branch share, a fixed stall per branch, a predictor that removes the stall only when it guesses right, and an accuracy percentage.
recognize.contrast: Branch penalty with a predictor is easy to confuse with a plain penalty on every branch; the accuracy tells you which fraction of branches still stall.

check.body: Count over 100 instructions. X1 spends 100 + 30 x 2 = 160 cycles. X2 has 30 branches, 6 of them mispredicted, so 100 + 6 x 2 = 112 cycles. The ratio 160 / 112 matches the CPI route.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2022 CS answer key, IIT Kharagpur (organising institute, named in the page banner), IIT Guwahati archive copy

hints.text: Which instructions can cause a wait, and in the improved machine which of those still pay it?
Cycles per instruction is the base value plus the average number of stall cycles each instruction brings.
Both machines run at the same clock, so the speed-up is just the ratio of their cycles per instruction.
For each machine, multiply the branch share, the share of branches that stall, and the stall length; add that to the base CPI.
In the old machine every branch stalls, so its extra cycles per instruction are the branch share times the stall length.

variation.stem: Processor A has a 5-stage pipeline with a base CPI of 1. In a program 40% of instructions are branches, and each branch causes a 3-cycle stall. Processor B has the same clock and a branch predictor that removes the stall for every correctly predicted branch, with no extra cost for wrong guesses. The predictor is 90% accurate. What is the speed-up of B over A, rounded to two decimal places?
variation.explanation: CPI of A is 1 + 0.4 x 3 = 2.2. For B only 10% of branches stall, so CPI is 1 + 0.4 x 0.1 x 3 = 1.12. The clocks match, so speed-up is 2.2 / 1.12 = 1.96. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
Consider a pipelined processor with 5 stages, Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Write Back (WB). Each stage of the pipeline, except the EX stage, takes one cycle. Assume that the ID stage merely decodes the instruction and the register read is performed in the EX stage. The EX stage takes one cycle for ADD instruction and two cycles for MUL instruction. Ignore pipeline register latencies.

Consider the following sequence of 8 instructions:

ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL

Assume that every MUL instruction is data-dependent on the ADD instruction just before it and every ADD instruction (except the first ADD) is data-dependent on the MUL instruction just before it. The Speedup is defined as follows:

Speedup = (Execution time without operand forwarding) / (Execution time with operand forwarding)

The Speedup achieved in executing the given instruction sequence on the pipelined processor (rounded to 2 decimal places) is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two pipeline charts for eight alternating ADD and MUL instructions: without forwarding the last WB is in cycle 30, with forwarding in cycle 16.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: Operand forwarding (bypassing) hands a result to the next instruction straight from the stage that produces it, instead of waiting until the result is written to the register file in WB. Here registers are read in EX, so a dependent instruction cannot start its EX before its operand is available. Without forwarding the operand is available only after the producer's WB cycle; with forwarding it is available right after the producer's EX ends. The rule: a dependent instruction starts EX in the cycle after the operand becomes available; instructions otherwise move in order, one at a time through EX.

steps.title: Without forwarding
steps.body: Instruction 1 (ADD): IF 1, ID 2, EX 3, MEM 4, WB 5. Instruction 2 (MUL) needs its result, so EX starts in cycle 6 and takes cycles 6-7, MEM 8, WB 9. Instruction 3 (ADD): EX 10, WB 12. Each later instruction starts EX right after the previous WB. WB cycles are 5, 9, 12, 16, 19, 23, 26, 30. The last instruction finishes in cycle 30.

steps.title: With forwarding
steps.body: Instruction 1 EX in cycle 3. Each next EX starts as soon as the previous EX ends, so EX units run back to back: 4 ADDs of 1 cycle and 4 MULs of 2 cycles are 12 cycles, cycles 3 to 14. Then MEM in 15 and WB in 16 for the last. Total 16 cycles.

steps.title: Speedup
steps.body: $30/16=1.875$, which rounds to 1.88. The official range is 1.87 to 1.88.

shortcut.body: With forwarding, EX runs without gaps: 2 cycles to reach EX, 12 EX cycles, 2 cycles after: 16. Without forwarding, each instruction after the first adds the wait for the producer's WB: 5 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 30. Divide.

traps.text: Letting the dependent instruction read in the very cycle of the producer's WB gives 23 cycles without forwarding and a speed-up of 1.44, outside the official range 1.87 to 1.88; the chart starts EX the cycle after WB.
Adding every instruction's own stages (8 x 5 plus the 4 extra MUL cycles = 44 cycles) as if nothing overlapped.
Treating the MUL as a 1-cycle EX shortens both totals (to 26 and 12 cycles in the same model) and changes the ratio; the 2-cycle EX must be kept.

recognize.clues: Registers read in EX, a longer EX for MUL, every instruction depending on the one just before it, and a speed-up comparing runs with and without forwarding.
recognize.contrast: A load-use stall also needs one bubble even with forwarding; here the delay comes from the multi-cycle EX stage and the producer-to-consumer gap, not from a memory load.

check.body: Second route, by EX start cycles. With forwarding the 8 EX phases run back to back from cycle 3: the ADDs start in cycles 3, 6, 9, 12 and the MULs in 4, 7, 10, 13, so the last MUL is in EX in cycles 13 and 14, MEM in 15, WB in 16. Without forwarding each EX starts the cycle after the producer's WB: 3, 6, 10, 13, 17, 20, 24, 27, so the last MUL is in EX in cycles 27 and 28, MEM in 29, WB in 30. Then 30/16 = 1.875 lies inside the official range 1.87 to 1.88.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2021 CS-2 answer key, IIT Bombay (organising institute), IIT Guwahati archive copy of the CS-1/CS-2 PDF

hints.text: In this machine, when does a dependent instruction first get to use the value it needs, with and without a bypass?
Forwarding passes a result straight from the stage that makes it; without it the value is usable only after the producer writes it back.
Registers are read in EX here, so a dependent instruction cannot begin EX until its operand exists.
Draw each instruction as five stages with the right EX length. For each dependent pair, place the consumer EX after the producer WB, then repeat with EX right after the producer EX.
The first ADD has no producer ahead of it, so its write back lands in cycle 5 under both models.

variation.stem: Consider a 5-stage pipeline with IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB. Every stage takes one cycle except EX, which takes 1 cycle for ADD and 3 cycles for MUL. The ID stage only decodes, and registers are read in EX. The sequence is ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, where every MUL depends on the ADD just before it and the second ADD depends on the first MUL. Speed-up is the time without operand forwarding divided by the time with it. What is the speed-up?
variation.explanation: Without forwarding, each dependent instruction starts EX after the producer WB: write backs fall in cycles 5, 10, 13 and 18. With forwarding the EX stage runs without gaps for 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 8 cycles, so the total is 2 + 8 + 2 = 12. The speed-up is 18 / 12 = 1.5. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
A five-stage pipeline has stage delays of 150, 120, 150, 160 and 140 nanoseconds. The registers that are used between the pipeline stages have a delay of 5 nanoseconds each.

The total time to execute 100 independent instructions on this pipeline, assuming there are no pipeline stalls, is ____________ nanoseconds.

solutionDiagram.alt: Space-time chart of a five-stage pipeline with 165 ns cycles; the 100th instruction completes in cycle 104, giving 17160 ns.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A pipeline stage is a part of instruction processing; a register between two stages holds the partial result and adds its own delay. All stages share one clock, so the period must cover the slowest stage plus the register delay. Independent instructions with no stalls enter one per cycle. For $k$ stages and $n$ instructions the pipeline needs $k+n-1$ cycles.

steps.title: Cycle time
steps.body: The slowest stage is 160 ns, and the register adds 5 ns.

shortcut.body: (5 + 99) x (160 + 5) = 104 x 165 = 17160. Unsafe only if a stall or a different register delay is mentioned.

traps.text: Forgetting the register delay gives 104 x 160 = 16640.
Using 100 x 165 = 16500 forgets the 4 cycles needed to fill the pipeline.
Using the sum of the stage delays as the cycle (720 ns) treats it as non-pipelined.

recognize.clues: Several unequal stage delays, a register delay between stages, independent instructions and no stalls.
recognize.contrast: It resembles a non-pipelined sum of delays; the phrase about pipeline stalls and registers between stages says the beat is the slowest stage plus the register.

check.body: Second route: the first instruction leaves after 5 x 165 = 825 ns, and each of the other 99 follows one beat later, so 825 + 99 x 165 = 825 + 16335 gives the same total.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2021 CS-1 answer key, IIT Bombay (organising institute), IIT Guwahati archive copy of the CS-1/CS-2 PDF

hints.text: What sets the length of one clock beat in this pipeline, given the stage delays and the registers between them?
A stage plus the register that follows it must fit in one beat, so the beat follows the slowest stage.
With independent instructions and no stalls, one instruction completes per beat after the pipe has filled.
Find the beat, then count the beats as the stages plus the other instructions, and multiply the two.

variation.stem: A four-stage pipeline has stage delays of 100, 130, 110 and 120 nanoseconds. The registers between the stages each have a delay of 10 nanoseconds. How long does it take, in nanoseconds, to execute 80 independent instructions with no pipeline stalls?
variation.explanation: The beat is the slowest stage plus a register: 130 + 10 = 140 ns. The pipeline needs 4 + 79 = 83 beats, and 83 x 140 = 11620 ns. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: Consider a non-pipelined processor operating at 2.5 GHz. It takes 5 clock cycles to complete an instruction. You are going to make a 5-stage pipeline out of this processor. Overheads associated with pipelining force you to operate the pipelined processor at 2 GHz. In a given program, assume that 30% are memory instructions, 60% are ALU instructions and the rest are branch instructions. 5% of the memory instructions cause stalls of 50 clock cycles each due to cache misses and 50% of the branch instructions cause stalls of 2 cycles each. Assume that there are no stalls associated with the execution of ALU instructions. For this program, the speedup achieved by the pipelined processor over the non-pipelined processor (round off to 2 decimal places) is ______.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: CPI is the average number of cycles per instruction; stalls add to it. Because the two processors have different clocks, compare time per instruction, which is CPI divided by frequency. Speed-up is the old time over the new time. The extra stall per instruction is the sum, over instruction classes, of fraction x probability of stalling x stall length.

steps.title: Non-pipelined time
steps.body: CPI 5 at 2.5 GHz: $5/2.5=2$ ns per instruction.

steps.title: Pipelined CPI
steps.body: Memory: $0.3\times0.05\times50=0.75$. Branch (the remaining 10%): $0.1\times0.5\times2=0.1$. ALU: 0. So CPI is $1+0.75+0.1=1.85$. At 2 GHz that is $1.85/2=0.925$ ns.

steps.title: Speed-up
steps.body: $2/0.925=2.162$, so 2.16. The official range is 2.15 to 2.18.

shortcut.body: Pipelined CPI = 1 + 0.75 + 0.1 = 1.85, time 1.85 / 2 = 0.925 ns; baseline 5 / 2.5 = 2 ns; ratio 2.16. Remember branches are 10%, not 30%.

traps.text: Using the branch share as 30% (the memory share) double counts and lowers the speed-up; branches are 100 - 30 - 60 = 10%.
Ignoring the clock change and dividing 5 / 1.85 = 2.70.
Applying the 50-cycle stall to all memory instructions instead of the 5% that miss gives a very large CPI and a tiny speed-up.

recognize.clues: Two different clock frequencies, instruction mix percentages with a missing branch share, and stalls that hit only some instructions of a class.
recognize.contrast: Speedup from pipelining alone is the stage count; here the slower clock and the stalls reduce it, so the real ratio of times must be computed.

check.body: Take 1000 instructions. Stall cycles are 300 x 0.05 x 50 = 750 plus 100 x 0.5 x 2 = 100, so 1850 cycles at 2 GHz is 925 ns. The old machine needs 5000 cycles at 2.5 GHz, which is 2000 ns. The ratio of these is the speed-up. Without stalls it would be 4, so a value below 4 is sensible.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi (organising institute), print of its paper-and-key web page, IIT Guwahati archive

hints.text: The two machines run at different clock rates, so what quantity can you compare fairly between them?
Time per instruction is cycles per instruction divided by the clock frequency; stalls raise the cycles per instruction.
Extra cycles per instruction from a class of instructions equal its share, times the share that stalls, times the stall length.
Work out the share of branches from the other two shares. Sum the memory and branch stall contributions onto a base CPI of 1 for the pipelined design.
The non-pipelined design takes 5 cycles on a 2.5 GHz clock, which fixes its time per instruction in ns.

variation.stem: A non-pipelined processor runs at 2 GHz and needs 4 clock cycles per instruction. A 4-stage pipelined version must run at 1.6 GHz because of overheads. In a program, 40% of instructions are memory instructions, 50% are ALU instructions and the rest are branches. 10% of memory instructions stall for 20 cycles each, 40% of branches stall for 3 cycles each, and ALU instructions never stall. What is the speed-up of the pipelined processor, rounded to two decimal places?
variation.explanation: Branches are 10%. Pipelined CPI is 1 + 0.4 x 0.1 x 20 + 0.1 x 0.4 x 3 = 1.92, which at 1.6 GHz is 1.2 ns. The non-pipelined time is 4 / 2 = 2 ns, so the speed-up is 2 / 1.2 = 1.67. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
The instruction pipeline of a RISC processor has the following stages: Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Perform Operation (PO) and Writeback (WB). The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for every instruction. Consider a sequence of 100 instructions. In the PO stage, 40 instructions take 3 clock cycles each, 35 instructions take 2 clock cycles each, and the remaining 25 instructions take 1 clock cycle each. Assume that there are no data hazards and no control hazards.

The number of clock cycles required for completion of execution of the sequence of instructions is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Pipeline chart of five instructions with PO times 3, 2, 1, 3, 1; the PO stage is busy in every cycle from 4 to 13 and the last WB is in cycle 14.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A stage can hold only one instruction at a time. When the PO stage needs 3 cycles for an instruction, the instructions behind it cannot enter PO and wait in earlier stages (the chart marks them "hold"). A bottleneck stage that is busy in every cycle sets the speed of the whole pipeline. The rule: if one stage is the bottleneck and is never idle, total time = the cycles before the first instruction reaches it + the sum of its busy cycles + the cycles after the last instruction leaves it.
steps.tex: T=\text{(stages before PO)}+\sum\text{PO cycles}+\text{(stages after PO)}

steps.title: Check that PO never idles
steps.body: The other stages take 1 cycle, never longer than any PO time, so the next instruction is always waiting at OF when PO finishes. PO therefore works back to back from the moment the first instruction reaches it, whatever the order of the 3, 2 and 1 cycle instructions. The chart shows five instructions with PO times 3, 2, 1, 3, 1, and PO is busy in every cycle from 4 to 13.

steps.title: Add up
steps.body: Total PO cycles: $40\times3+35\times2+25\times1=120+70+25=215$. Before PO the first instruction spends IF, ID, OF: 3 cycles. After PO the last instruction spends 1 cycle in WB.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The sequence needs 219 cycles. A cycle-by-cycle simulation of 300 random orders of the 100 instructions gave 219 every time, so the order does not matter.

shortcut.body: Find the bottleneck stage (PO), add its total busy cycles (215), then add the 3 cycles before it and 1 after: 219. Safe because every other stage takes 1 cycle; unsafe if another stage could be longer than PO for some instruction.

traps.text: Using (5 + 99) = 104 cycles assumes every stage takes 1 cycle and ignores the extra PO time.
Adding all stage times of every instruction (100 x 4 + 215 = 615) counts the stages as if there were no overlap.
Writing 215 + 5 = 220 counts all five stages once more; the 215 already contains the PO stage, so only IF, ID, OF (3) and WB (1) are added.

recognize.clues: One stage whose time differs from instruction to instruction, all other stages at one cycle, and no hazards, so only the long stage matters.
recognize.contrast: Ordinary pipeline timing uses k + n - 1 cycles with equal stages; a variable-latency stage means the cycles of that stage add up instead.

check.body: Second route: with every PO taking 1 cycle the run would need 5 + 99 = 104 cycles. Each extra PO cycle then adds exactly one cycle, and there are 40 x 2 + 35 x 1 = 115 extras, giving 104 + 115.

sources.label: GATE Overflow discussion and solutions
GATE 2018 CS final answer key (organised by IIT Guwahati), gateexam.info copy

hints.text: Which stage can hold up the others, and does the order of the slow and fast instructions affect the total?
A stage serves one instruction at a time, so a slow stage makes the later instructions wait behind it.
If one stage is never idle, the total time is the time before the first instruction reaches it, plus all its busy cycles, plus the time after the last one leaves.
Add the PO cycles of every instruction, then add the stages that come before PO for the first instruction and after PO for the last.

variation.stem: A RISC pipeline has stages IF, ID, OF, PO and WB. IF, ID, OF and WB take 1 cycle for every instruction. In a sequence of 60 instructions, 20 take 4 cycles in PO, 25 take 2 cycles and the remaining 15 take 1 cycle. There are no data or control hazards. How many clock cycles does the sequence need to complete?
variation.explanation: PO is the busy stage and never idles. Its total is 20 x 4 + 25 x 2 + 15 x 1 = 145 cycles. Add 3 cycles for IF, ID and OF of the first instruction and 1 for the last WB: 145 + 4 = 149. A simulation over 200 random orders gave 149 each time. Generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
Instruction execution in a processor is divided into 5 stages, Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Execute (EX), and Write Back (WB). These stages take 5, 4, 20, 10, and 3 nanoseconds (ns) respectively. A pipelined implementation of the processor requires buffering between each pair of consecutive stages with a delay of 2 ns. Two pipelined implementations of the processor are contemplated:

(i) a naive pipeline implementation (NP) with 5 stages and
(ii) an efficient pipeline (EP) where the OF stage is divided into stages OF1 and OF2 with execution times of 12 ns and 8 ns respectively.

The speedup (correct to two decimal places) achieved by EP over NP in executing 20 independent instructions with no hazards is __________ .

solutionDiagram.alt: Bar charts of the stage delays of NP and EP with the dashed line at the slowest stage; cycles are 22 ns and 14 ns, giving 528 ns and 350 ns.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A pipeline clock cycle must be as long as the slowest stage plus the buffer (latch) delay. Splitting a long stage into two shorter ones shortens the cycle but adds one more stage to fill. Independent instructions with no hazards enter one per cycle, so $n$ instructions through $k$ stages take $k+n-1$ cycles. Speed-up of EP over NP is the NP time divided by the EP time.

steps.title: NP
steps.body: Slowest stage is OF at 20 ns, so the cycle is $20+2=22$ ns. Five stages and 20 instructions: $5+19=24$ cycles.

steps.title: EP
steps.body: Stages are 5, 4, 12, 8, 10, 3. The slowest is 12 ns, so the cycle is $12+2=14$ ns. Six stages: $6+19=25$ cycles.

steps.title: Speed-up
steps.body: $528/350=1.5086$, so 1.51. The official range is 1.49 to 1.52.

shortcut.body: Find the cycle of each design (22 and 14 ns), the cycle counts (24 and 25) and divide: 24 x 22 / (25 x 14).

traps.text: Ignoring the 2 ns buffer gives (24 x 20) / (25 x 12) = 1.60.
Using the same 24 cycles for both designs forgets that EP has six stages (25 cycles), giving 22 / 14 = 1.57.
Using the sum of stage delays (non-pipelined time) as the NP baseline; the question compares the two pipelines.

recognize.clues: Two pipelines compared on a finite number of instructions, a buffer delay between stages, and one stage split into two shorter ones.
recognize.contrast: For a very long run the speed-up tends to the ratio of the beats; with only 20 instructions the extra stage of the split design matters and lowers the ratio.

check.body: Second route: NP finishes the first instruction at 5 x 22 = 110 ns and 19 more follow 22 ns apart, 110 + 418 = 528. EP finishes it at 6 x 14 = 84 ns, then 19 x 14 = 266 more, 350. Long-run ratio 22 / 14 = 1.57 exceeds the result, as expected for a finite run.

hints.text: What does splitting one slow stage change about the clock beat, and what does it cost in the number of stages?
The beat is the slowest stage plus the buffer delay, and the stage count adds fill time for the first instruction.
Total time is the number of beats, stages plus instructions minus one, multiplied by the beat; the ratio of two designs is the speed-up.
List the stage delays of each design, take the largest, add the buffer, and compute the beat count for 20 instructions in each.
The naive design has five stages and its largest delay is the operand fetch.

variation.stem: A processor splits instruction execution into 5 stages that take 6, 3, 18, 9 and 4 ns. Each pair of consecutive stages needs a buffer with a delay of 1 ns. A naive pipeline (NP) uses the 5 stages. An efficient pipeline (EP) divides the 18 ns stage into two stages of 10 ns and 8 ns. What is the speed-up of EP over NP for 30 independent instructions with no hazards, rounded to two decimal places?
variation.explanation: NP has a beat of 18 + 1 = 19 ns and needs 5 + 29 = 34 cycles, so 646 ns. EP has a largest stage of 10 ns, a beat of 11 ns and needs 6 + 29 = 35 cycles, so 385 ns. The speed-up is 646 / 385 = 1.68. Generated for practice, not an exam question.
